query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: During elevated‐temperature exposure, degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by the selective oxidation of reactive elements (primarily Al, Cr, and Ti) at grain boundaries, which forms brittle, intergranular oxide phases that locally deplete strengthening elements. When these oxide–matrix interfaces cannot sustain thermal/mechanical stresses, they act as crack initiation sites that rapidly propagate, leading to catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous fcc matrix and minimal pre-existing oxide contamination.
generation.intervention: Switch the exposure gas from a strongly oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air or high oxygen partial pressure) to a moderately reducing environment (e.g., a controlled CO/H2 mixture) while keeping temperature and time constant.
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (e.g., above 700°C) under well-controlled oxidizing versus reducing gas atmospheres for durations sufficient to allow significant oxide formation (on the order of tens of hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of discrete, brittle Al/Cr/Ti-rich oxide precipitates, particularly along grain boundaries, which causes local elemental depletion in the matrix.
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing atmospheres, the reactive elements in the alloy preferentially oxidize and segregate to grain boundaries, creating brittle oxide phases that weaken intergranular cohesion. In reducing environments, the suppressed oxidation alters the kinetics, resulting in less pronounced oxide formation. The catastrophic failure is triggered when the brittle, oxidation-induced intergranular regions crack under thermal and/or mechanical stresses, compromising the structural integrity of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, one should observe the rapid development of intergranular oxide phases (detectable via microscopy and elemental mapping) along with evidence of local depletion of Al, Cr, and Ti near grain boundaries, accompanied by a lower fracture toughness and a tendency toward abrupt, catastrophic failure. Under reducing conditions, oxide formation will be less extensive, leading to a more uniform degradation profile and improved retention of bulk mechanical properties compared to the oxidizing baseline.
generation.baseline: The initial, unexposed state with a homogeneous fcc matrix and negligible oxidation in the as-manufactured alloy.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for high-temperature exposures (e.g., >700°C) and exposure durations where oxidation kinetics are significant (e.g., tens of hours) with gas environments ranging from strongly oxidizing to moderately reducing.
generation.uncertainty: The specific roles and quantitative contributions of individual elements (Al, Cr, and Ti) to the oxidation process, as well as the exact oxygen partial pressure threshold that triggers the transition to catastrophic failure, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples. Expose one set to a strongly oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air with high O2 partial pressure) and the other set to a moderately reducing gas mixture (e.g., CO/H2) at a fixed elevated temperature (e.g., 750°C) for an identical duration. Perform detailed microstructural analyses (using SEM, TEM, and EDX) to characterize oxide phase formation and elemental distributions, and conduct mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or fracture toughness testing) to assess failure modes.
measurements: Microstructural imaging (SEM/TEM) for oxide morphology and distribution
Elemental mapping (EDX) to detect depletion zones near oxides
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to identify oxide phases
Mechanical testing to determine changes in fracture toughness and failure mode
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing and reducing exposures produce similar oxide characteristics (i.e., no significant difference in the presence or distribution of intergranular oxides and elemental depletion), and if both sets of samples exhibit comparable mechanical performance and failure modes without a pronounced catastrophic failure in the oxidizing condition, then the hypothesis that selective oxidation governs degradation and catastrophic failure is falsified.
